File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-01 3 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Researching OpenClaw vulnerabilities, malicious skills and other security issues with the popular agent, and providing tips on how to mitigate them.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files
OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter process (node/python/deno/bun) resolving or connecting to api.telegram.org — the C2/exfil channel used by the malicious ClawHub skill cluster (polymarketbtc family) to ship stolen tokens and crypto keys out. Article-specific because it ties the agent runtime, not a browser, to Telegram Bot API egress. Rationale: api.telegram.org / t.me are the concrete C2 domains for the polymarketbtc ClawHub skill cluster (krajekisbtc) that exfiltrated tokens/keys; scoping the egress to agent interpreters (node/python/deno/bun) rather than browsers is what makes it article-specific and low-noise. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/researchers-find-341-malicious-clawhub.html • https://cofense.com/blog/weaponizing-telegram-bots-how-threat-actors-exfiltrate-credentials • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a legitimate node/python Telegram bot library for a sanctioned notification bot
  • CI/CD runner posting build status to a corporate Telegram channel via curl
  • Security researcher testing Telegram Bot API integrations in a sandbox
  • Personal productivity script the user knowingly runs that pushes alerts to t.me
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("corp-notify-bot","ci-status") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — identify the skill/script driving the agent and whether the Telegram bot token is hardcoded; correlate to any SKILL.md or config the agent loaded in the prior 10 min. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, rotate all tokens/keys reachable from that host (Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, Slack OAuth, cloud creds, git tokens), and block api.telegram.org egress for non-approved hosts. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same agent runtime touching Telegram, and for reads of .env/credentials files by the same runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has "t.me"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "telegram.org" or Name == "t.me"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter (node/python/deno/bun) spawning a shell whose command line touches secret stores — .env, cloud credential files, SSH keys, .npmrc, or provider API-key variables. Grounded in the article's note that agents keep tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent, which malicious skills harvest via embedded bash. Rationale: The article states agents store tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent and that malicious skills harvest them via embedded bash; scoping parent=agent-runtime + child=shell + a secret-store string in the cmdline is the concrete high-fidelity pivot corroborated by Snyk's OpenClaw credential-leak research. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/openclaw-skills-credential-leaks-research/ • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate skill loading a .env for a sanctioned integration (e.g. a deployment helper reading credentials it is authorized to use)
  • Developer debugging an agent locally and grepping their own .npmrc / .env
  • DevOps automation that echoes an API-key variable name (not value) during setup
  • Package-manager install (npm/pip) that touches .npmrc as part of normal auth
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent agent's loaded skill/config — determine whether the secret access is part of a sanctioned skill or an untrusted ClawHub skill pulled recently. 2) Contain: suspend the agent, quarantine the skill file, and rotate every credential the command referenced (cloud, git, provider API keys, Telegram/Slack tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host+user for outbound connections to api.telegram.org / paste sites shortly after (join to UC1), and sweep other hosts running the same skill hash/name.

Azure CLI Password Spray Hits at Least 78 Microsoft Accounts in 81M+ Attempts

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 8 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a "massive, ongoing, automated password spray attack" aimed at Microsoft's Azure command-line interface (CLI), compromising dozens of accounts in the process. The activity, per Huntress, originates from an IPv6 address range (2a0a:d683::/32) controlled by internet infrastructure provider LSHIY LLC (AS32167). "Between June 12 and June 26, the threat

Successful Azure CLI sign-in from LSHIY LLC IPv6 range (2a0a:d683::/32) — confirmed compromise AIExploitation High
Hunts for successful Entra sign-ins to the first-party Azure CLI app (04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46) originating from the LSHIY LLC attacker infrastructure (2a0a:d683::/32, AS32167/AS955). Any success from this range against this app equals a confirmed account takeover from the ongoing LSHIY password-spray campaign, so it is the sharpest post-compromise pivot. Rationale: Uses three high-fidelity article IOCs together: the Azure CLI app ID 04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46, the LSHIY LLC IPv6 range 2a0a:d683::/32 and its ASNs (32167/955), plus a success result — a combination with effectively no benign explanation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5847440/unable-to-authenticate-azure-cli-for-frontdoor-con
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate user or admin whose ISP is (mis)attributed to AS32167/AS955 in the geo-IP feed
  • Corporate egress or cloud automation NAT'd through an IPv6 address that overlaps the range (unlikely — dedicated attacker infra)
  • Threat-intel/red-team validation testing intentionally sourced from the same range
  • Delayed/replayed sign-in log ingestion causing a stale success to re-surface
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the UPN, IP and app; pull the user's full SigninLogs for the prior 14 days to see the preceding failed-spray attempts and any other successful IPs. 2) Contain: Immediately revoke all refresh/access tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force a password reset, and disable the account until identity is re-verified; block 2a0a:d683::/32 at the CA named-location/IP layer. 3) Hunt: Enumerate every account with any auth (success or fail) from AS32167/AS955, review post-login Azure activity (AzureActivity, role/app-consent changes) for the compromised identity, and audit CA policies for the ROPC gap.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")               // LSHIY LLC (AS32167) range
| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful auth = compromise
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthenticationRequirement, IsInteractive, ResourceDisplayName
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (32167, 955) or ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")   // LSHIY LLC infrastructure
| where ResultType == "0"                                 // successful sign-in = compromise
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserId, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Location, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthenticationRequirement, IsInteractive, ResourceDisplayName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Azure CLI ROPC password spray from LSHIY LLC (2a0a:d683::/32) — high failed-auth fan-out AIExploitation High
Detects the password-spray phase: a burst of failed Entra sign-ins to the Azure CLI app from the LSHIY LLC infrastructure hitting many distinct accounts per hour. This is the article's 81M-attempt credential-spray behaviour, scoped to the attacker's app + network IOCs so it fires before a spray converts to compromise. Rationale: Combines the Azure CLI app ID, the LSHIY IPv6 range/ASNs and a >=5 distinct-account-per-hour fan-out on failures — the defining shape of the campaign's password spray (bad-password 50126 / lockout 50053) rather than a single-account brute force. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html
ATT&CKT1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A broken CI/CD pipeline or SDK using stale Azure CLI credentials generating repeated 50126s (but from corporate IP, not AS32167)
  • Geo-IP misattribution folding a benign ISP into AS32167/AS955
  • Password-manager mass-rotation failures across many service accounts from one host
  • Sign-in log ingestion backfill inflating the hourly count for a single window
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the SampleUsers set — confirm they are real tenant identities and check whether any subsequently show ResultType 0 (successful compromise) from the same range. 2) Contain: Add 2a0a:d683::/32 (and AS32167/AS955) to a CA block named-location and enable the userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired setting to block ROPC; pre-emptively force password reset on any sprayed account confirmed to use a breached/unrotated password. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'Successful Azure CLI sign-in from LSHIY' to catch conversions, and search other apps/ASNs for the same fan-out pattern (campaign spans multiple ASNs).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")               // LSHIY LLC (AS32167) range
| where ErrorCode != 0                                            // failed spray attempts
| summarize FailedAttempts=count(), TargetedAccounts=dcount(AccountObjectId), SampleUsers=make_set(AccountUpn, 15), ErrorCodes=make_set(ErrorCode, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), IPAddress
| where TargetedAccounts >= 5     // 5 = spray fan-out floor; single-user brute stays below
| order by FailedAttempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (32167, 955) or ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")   // LSHIY LLC infrastructure
| where ResultType != "0"                                 // failed spray attempts
| summarize FailedAttempts=count(), TargetedAccounts=dcount(UserId), SampleUsers=make_set(UserPrincipalName, 15), ResultTypes=make_set(ResultType, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), IPAddress
| where TargetedAccounts >= 5     // 5 = spray fan-out floor; single-user brute stays below
| order by FailedAttempts desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:"Microsoft Azure CLI" @properties.status.errorCode:(50126 OR 50053 OR 50055) CIDR(@network.client.ip, 2a0a:d683::/32)
CLOUD

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where cidrmatch("2a0a:d683::/32", src) AND targeted_users>=5
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - failed_attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as failed_attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as targeted_users, values(Authentication.user) as users, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Microsoft Azure CLI" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where cidrmatch("2a0a:d683::/32", src) AND targeted_users>=5
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - failed_attempts
Azure CLI ROPC sign-in bypassing Conditional Access (CA NotApplied, non-interactive) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the systemic weakness the campaign abuses: successful non-interactive Azure CLI (ROPC) sign-ins where Conditional Access was NotApplied — i.e. the legacy ROPC /token flow slipped past CAP because policy never evaluated. Catches this bypass tenant-wide regardless of source IP, surfacing exposure even from future attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core mechanism — ROPC to the Azure CLI app (04b07795-...) succeeding with ConditionalAccessStatus=notApplied — which is exactly how the campaign slipped past MFA/CAP; scoping to non-interactive + this app keeps it tied to the specific bypass rather than generic sign-ins. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers/automation using `az login` with username/password (ROPC) from unmanaged scripts where no CA policy targets Azure CLI
  • Service/break-glass accounts intentionally excluded from CA that use Azure CLI
  • Pipelines running Azure CLI from an agent not covered by any CA assignment
  • Tenants that simply have no CA policy scoped to the Azure CLI app (the very gap being hunted) generating expected-but-risky volume
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$" and AccountUpn !has "break-glass" and AccountUpn !has "svc-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each UPN, confirm whether the source IPs are corporate/known-automation or unfamiliar (cross-check against 2a0a:d683::/32 and other spray ASNs); benign ROPC from corp IPs is exposure, ROPC from unknown IPs is likely compromise. 2) Contain: Close the gap — extend CA to All Cloud Apps + All Client App types and enable userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired to block ROPC; revoke sessions for any UPN with unfamiliar-IP ROPC success. 3) Hunt: List all identities using ROPC/Azure CLI to size migration off the legacy flow, and correlate these UPNs against the LSHIY spray failed-auth set to spot pre-compromise targeting.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful token issuance
| where IsInteractive == false                                    // ROPC is non-interactive
| where ConditionalAccessStatus =~ "notApplied"                   // CAP never evaluated = bypass
| summarize SignIns=count(), Countries=make_set(Country, 10), IPs=make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, ClientAppUsed
| order by SignIns desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ResultType == "0"                                 // successful token issuance
| where ConditionalAccessStatus =~ "notApplied"          // CAP never evaluated = ROPC bypass
| summarize SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, UserId, ClientAppUsed, AppDisplayName
| order by SignIns desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Critical

Researcher Analyzes 3,000 Live ClickFix Payloads, Exposing API-Driven Malware Delivery

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

ClickFix, the trick that fools people into running malware by hand, has quietly grown a back office. New research shows the malicious commands behind its fake "prove you're human" pages are now handed out by API-driven servers that give each visitor the same malware in a different disguise. The same research also turned up a new delivery method built to slip past Windows' script scanning.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix launcher: explorer/WindowsTerminal spawning powershell/cmd/msiexec with immediate network egress · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Researcher Analyzes 3,000 Live ClickFix Payloads, Exposing API-Driven Malware De
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ClickFix Downloads-folder AMSI-bypass orchestrator (Move-Item Downloads -> tar -xf -> conhost --headless) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Contact to ClickFix API payload-delivery servers (comicstar.lat / babybon.cfd / merkantalolol.asia) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ClickFix launcher: explorer/WindowsTerminal spawning powershell/cmd/msiexec with immediate network egress AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the ClickFix paste-and-run process chain identified as the dependable signal in Pals' 3,000-payload dataset: explorer.exe (Win+R lure) or WindowsTerminal.exe/OpenConsole.exe (the newer Win+X lure) launching a script interpreter that reaches a public IP right after. Article-specific because it targets the exact launcher set (PowerShell/cmd/msiexec, the top-3 launchers at ~39/39/34%) tied to the Win+X shift that leaves no RunMRU trace. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly named 'dependable signal' — explorer.exe/WindowsTerminal.exe launching powershell/cmd/msiexec then hitting the network — with the exact top-3 launcher set (PowerShell/cmd/msiexec at 39/39/34%) and the Win+X Terminal pivot. Cross-checked Microsoft's ClickFix analysis and Pals' OrangeCon writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/08/21/think-before-you-clickfix-analyzing-the-clickfix-social-engineering-technique/ • https://github.com/bert-janp • https://cybercentaurs.com/blog/deconstructing-the-clickfix-infection-chain-part-2-loader-obfuscation-and-stealth-persistence/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Windows Terminal (Win+X) to run a PowerShell/curl script that legitimately downloads from a public package registry
  • IT admin pasting a remediation one-liner into an elevated terminal that fetches a vendor tool
  • msiexec.exe pulling an MSI from a public software vendor URL during user-initiated install
  • PowerShell profile or module auto-update reaching a public endpoint at terminal launch
  • Browser/help-desk workflow launching a signed installer via explorer that phones home for licensing
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("winget","choco","scoop","\\git\\","npm ","pip install","Update-Module"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP set; check whether the parent chain originated from a browser-driven paste (no script file on disk) versus a known installer. Verify the destination against threat intel — especially the payload-server domains. 2) CONTAIN: If the command line shows in-memory/obfuscated execution or an unknown public destination, isolate the device and kill the interpreter process tree. 3) HUNT: Sweep the same user/host for the Downloads-folder orchestrator (UC2) and for DNS/connections to comicstar.lat, babybon.cfd, merkantalolol.asia within 24h either side.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","msiexec.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","OpenConsole.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("winget","choco","scoop","\\git\\","npm ","pip install"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Dests=make_set(RemoteUrl, 20), any(RemoteIP)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessParentFileName, Interpreter=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","OpenConsole.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","msiexec.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("winget","choco","scoop","\\git\\","npm ","pip install"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.exe OR *\\WindowsTerminal.exe OR *\\windowsterminal.exe OR *\\OpenConsole.exe) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(explorer|WindowsTerminal|OpenConsole)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|msiexec)\.exe$/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/(winget|choco|scoop|\\git\\|npm |pip install)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

ClickFix Downloads-folder AMSI-bypass orchestrator (Move-Item Downloads -> tar -xf -> conhost --headless) AIInstallation High
Hunts the newer ClickFix delivery Pals disclosed that sidesteps AMSI: the pasted clipboard line is only a harmless-looking orchestrator that moves a pre-downloaded zip out of the Downloads folder to %TMP%, extracts it with tar, and runs the real script hidden via conhost --headless. The payload itself never touches the clipboard/AMSI, so this string-triad is the highest-fidelity anchor available. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim orchestrator from the article (Move-Item $HOME\Downloads -> $env:TMP, tar -xf, conhost --headless powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File, with the 'I am not a robot reCAPTCHA Verification ID' decoy comment). The Move-Item+Downloads+tar+-xf triad in a single PowerShell invocation is not benign admin behaviour. conhost --headless corroborated by cybercentaurs' ClickFix loader analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://cybercentaurs.com/blog/deconstructing-the-clickfix-infection-chain-part-2-loader-obfuscation-and-stealth-persistence/ • https://github.com/bert-janp
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1562.001 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer script that genuinely relocates a downloaded release archive to a temp build dir and untars it (rare in one PowerShell line with Move-Item)
  • Backup/migration tooling that consolidates user Downloads into an archive staging area
  • Legitimate installer wrapper that stages a tar/zip from Downloads before extraction
  • Security researcher reproducing ClickFix in a sandbox on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","OpenConsole.exe","cmd.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("conhost --headless","-ExecutionPolicy Bypass","reCAPTCHA")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Recover the staged archive path in %TMP% and the extracted .ps1; hash and detonate the extracted script — the orchestrator is benign, the dropped file is the malware. Confirm a file recently landed in the user's Downloads folder via browser (DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the powershell/conhost tree, quarantine the archive and extracted script from both Downloads and %TMP%. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the extracted script's outbound connections and check the org for connections to comicstar.lat / babybon.cfd / merkantalolol.asia and for the UC1 launcher chain on other hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Move-Item"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Downloads"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "tar"
    and ProcessCommandLine contains "-xf"
| extend AmsiBypassMarker = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("conhost --headless","-ExecutionPolicy Bypass","reCAPTCHA Verification","I am not a robot")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AmsiBypassMarker, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "Move-Item"
    and ActingProcessCommandLine has "Downloads"
    and ActingProcessCommandLine has "tar"
    and ActingProcessCommandLine contains "-xf"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Downloads-folder AMSI-bypass orchestrator one-liner
id: 5a3f1c2e-8b47-4d16-9e02-7c4a1f9b6d33
description: Detects the ClickFix orchestrator clipboard line that moves a pre-downloaded archive out of the Downloads folder to TEMP, extracts it with tar, and runs the payload hidden via conhost --headless to avoid AMSI script scanning.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researcher-analyzes-3000-live-clickfix.html
  - https://cybercentaurs.com/blog/deconstructing-the-clickfix-infection-chain-part-2-loader-obfuscation-and-stealth-persistence/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1204.004
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'Move-Item'
      - 'Downloads'
      - 'tar'
      - '-xf'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) (@CommandLine:*Move-Item* OR @CommandLine:*move-item*) (@CommandLine:*Downloads* OR @CommandLine:*downloads*) (@CommandLine:*tar\ -xf* OR @CommandLine:*conhost\ --headless*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)Move-Item", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)Downloads", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)tar\\s+-xf|conhost\\s+--headless", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Move-Item*" AND Processes.process="*Downloads*" AND Processes.process="*tar*" AND Processes.process="*-xf*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Move-Item*" AND Processes.process="*Downloads*" AND Processes.process="*tar*" AND Processes.process="*-xf*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Contact to ClickFix API payload-delivery servers (comicstar.lat / babybon.cfd / merkantalolol.asia) AICommand & Control High
Alerts on any host resolving or connecting to the ClickFix on-demand payload servers Pals named, plus the ClickFix lure/delivery domains pre-extracted for this campaign. Per the article, a hit means a malicious command was almost certainly placed in that user's clipboard — a direct pre-execution warning even before the paste-and-run fires. Rationale: comicstar.lat, babybon.cfd and merkantalolol.asia are the three payload servers named in the article and independently tracked in ThreatFox IOC feeds; the remaining domains are the campaign's pre-extracted ClickFix lure/delivery hosts. Domain resolution is a clean pre-paste warning signal per Pals' own guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/threatfox-iocs-for-2026-06-08-7e3d1405 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/08/21/think-before-you-clickfix-analyzing-the-clickfix-social-engineering-technique/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1204.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team detonating ClickFix samples in a monitored sandbox that shares telemetry with production
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing to the lure domain for research from a corporate host
  • DNS sinkhole / secure web gateway pre-resolving the domain for blocking (check source is the proxy, not an endpoint)
  • Typosquat collision where a benign new registration reuses one of these short ccTLD labels (validate against current ThreatFox status)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the host/user and the process that made the request (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName). Determine if it was a browser (lure page loaded) vs. an interpreter (payload already fetching). Confirm the domain is still live-malicious in ThreatFox. 2) CONTAIN: Block the seven domains at the DNS/proxy layer org-wide; if an interpreter (not a browser) made the call, isolate the host. 3) HUNT: On the identified host, look back 1h for the UC1 launcher chain and UC2 Downloads orchestrator, and forward-sweep all hosts that resolved any of these domains in the last 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("comicstar.lat","babybon.cfd","merkantalolol.asia","serviceverifycaptcho.com","ostatniaposlugarumia.pl","upload.admedia.org","babjon.ch")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("comicstar.lat","babybon.cfd","merkantalolol.asia","serviceverifycaptcho.com","ostatniaposlugarumia.pl","upload.admedia.org","babjon.ch")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Citrix Patches Six NetScaler Flaws Allowing File Read and Denial-of-Service

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 11 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Citrix on Tuesday released security updates to address multiple flaws in NetScaler ADC (formerly Citrix ADC) and NetScaler Gateway (formerly Citrix Gateway) that could be exploited by an attacker to facilitate arbitrary file reads or trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-8451 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An insufficient input validation

Citrix NetScaler SAML pre-auth memory overread exploitation (CVE-2026-8451 / CVE-2026-3055) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts bursts of POST requests to the NetScaler SAML IDP endpoint /saml/login from a single internet source, characteristic of the watchTowr overread technique that repeatedly varies request length to squeeze a few bytes of process memory per response (leaked via the NSC_TASS cookie). Article-specific: anchors on the exact SAML IDP attack surface and the length-fuzzing behaviour rather than any generic web attack. Rationale: Anchors on the exact watchTowr-confirmed endpoint (POST /saml/login, SAMLRequest param, AssertionConsumerServiceURL abuse leaking memory in the NSC_TASS cookie) plus the technique's tell: many varied-length requests from a single source. defender_kql/falcon/datadog/cloudwatch left empty because a NetScaler ADC/Gateway appliance ships no Defender XDR, FDR, or CloudTrail telemetry — its HTTP logs reach the SOC only via CEF/syslog (Sentinel CommonSecurityLog) or a fronting proxy (Splunk Web). Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/citrixbleed-to-infinity-and-beyond-citrix-netscaler-pre-auth-memory-overread-cve-2026-8451/ • https://cyberscoop.com/citrix-netscaler-flaw-cve-2026-8451-citrixbleed/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-8451
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Large enterprise behind a single NAT/egress IP generating many legitimate /saml/login POSTs
  • Synthetic monitoring or load-testing repeatedly probing the SAML endpoint
  • SSO storm after a mass session expiry or IdP outage recovery
  • Partner/federated IdP health-check probes hitting the ACS endpoint from one fixed source
Suppression filter
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false   // keep only internet-facing sources; overread is pre-auth external
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull raw requests from the top SourceIP and inspect the SAMLRequest bodies for malformed XML — unterminated AssertionConsumerServiceURL=, a missing '>' on <samlp:AuthnRequest>, or a test Issuer like 'watchtowr'; check response sizes / NSC_TASS cookie length for anomalies. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter and confirm the appliance is on a fixed build (14.1-72.61, 13.1-63.18, or the relevant FIPS/NDcPP release); if not, prioritise emergency patch. 3) Hunt: pivot to CVE-2026-10816 arbitrary-file-read attempts against the management interface (NSIP/SNIP), review config-file access, and rotate any credentials/secrets that could have been in leaked memory.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let SamlBurstThreshold = 50;   // legit users hit /saml/login a few times; 50+ POSTs from ONE external source in 1h fits the length-varying overread fuzz loop
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" and DeviceProduct has "NetScaler"
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false   // pre-auth overread is internet-facing; drop internal SSO traffic
| summarize RequestCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Appliances = dcount(DestinationIP), SampleUrl = any(RequestURL) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where RequestCount > SamlBurstThreshold
| order by RequestCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Surfaces assets still carrying any of the six CVEs from Citrix's July 2026 NetScaler bulletin (CVE-2026-8451/8452/8655/10816/10817/13474) so exposure is closed before exploitation. Article-specific: keys on the exact CVE set and fixed builds (14.1-72.61 / 13.1-63.18) rather than a generic outdated-software check. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE identifiers from the Citrix bulletin as high-fidelity match keys against vuln-management telemetry; fixed builds (14.1-72.61 / 13.1-63.18) are cited in the runbook so operators know the remediation target. Empty datadog/falcon/cloudwatch because vuln-posture data for a NetScaler appliance does not live in those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/citrix-security-advisory-av26-645 • https://vuldb.com/cve/CVE-2026-13474 • https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2026-10816
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM/scanner version-detection lag flagging an already-patched appliance until the next scan
  • Decommissioned NetScaler still present in inventory
  • FIPS/NDcPP build version mapping differing from mainline (14.1-72.61-FIPS / 13.1-37.272) causing mismatched patch status
  • NetScaler Console (management plane) misidentified as a vulnerable ADC data-plane instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each hit's SoftwareVersion is genuinely below the fixed build (14.1-72.61, 13.1-63.18, or the matching FIPS/NDcPP release) and note which CVEs apply given the appliance role (SAML IDP, Gateway/AAA vserver, LB-Oracle/DNS, HTTP/2). 2) Contain: schedule the upgrade; for CVE-2026-13474 also set Http2SmallWndTimeout to 30s (non-strict HTTP profiles default to 0 and upgrade alone does not fix them), and restrict management access on NSIP/Cluster Management IP/SNIP to close CVE-2026-10816. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these appliances against the SAML-overread detection to see if any exposed asset is already being probed.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")

| sort - files

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phantom Squatting: AI-Hallucinated Domains as a Software Supply Chain Vector

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-01 10 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers can exploit LLM domain hallucinations through phantom squatting to target supply chains. Read the analysis to learn more. The post Phantom Squatting: AI-Hallucinated Domains as a Software Supply Chain Vector appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP + companion APK by SHA256 on endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the two Unit 42-published Montana Empire artifacts landing on managed endpoints: the 7,958,528-byte kit ZIP (postal-service brand clone with PHP backend + Telegram C2) and the 12,649,472-byte malicious 'post' APK. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact file hashes rather than any generic phishing behaviour. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 hashes Unit 42 published for the Montana Empire kit ZIP (7,958,528 bytes) and companion [redacted]post.apk (12,649,472 bytes); both hashes were independently confirmed on the origin-unit42 mirror and CyberPress write-up, so they meet the two-source bar. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256, the landing path, and the InitiatingProcess/User that wrote or ran it; verify the host is not a known malware-analysis sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine/delete the ZIP and APK, and block both hashes org-wide via custom IOC. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process and user to any browser/email download source, look for the kit's PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) or Telegram (api.telegram.org) egress, and check whether the APK was forwarded to other users.

Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the Montana Empire kit's distinctive server-side PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) being written to disk or requested over HTTP, indicating the postal-service phishing clone is being staged or is live on infrastructure you can see. Article-specific because these three filenames are the kit's internal component names, not generic web paths. Rationale: Pivots on the three exact PHP component names Unit 42/CyberPress attribute to the Montana Empire kit (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php); these are non-generic internal filenames, so a file-create or IIS request for them is high-fidelity for kit staging on visible infra. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named panel_track.php in an unrelated in-house web app
  • Pen-test / red-team dropping a lookalike phishing kit during an authorised exercise
  • WAF or scanner replaying kit URIs against your site (request hits with 404s, no file on disk)
  • Security researcher unpacking the kit ZIP on an analysis host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hit is a file-write (kit staged locally) vs an inbound IIS request (external probing); check the folder path, writing process, and HTTP status. 2) Contain: if written to your web root, take the site offline / remove the files and preserve a forensic copy; if inbound-only, block the source IP and confirm no 200 responses. 3) Hunt: look for the kit ZIP hash on the same host, outbound connections to api.telegram.org (kit C2), and any web-shell-style process (php/w3wp spawning cmd/powershell).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
