AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the article's core TTP: an AI coding assistant / agent process (Cursor, VS Code+Copilot, Windsurf, Ollama, etc.) making an outbound connection or DNS query to an external domain the org has never seen before — the moment an LLM-hallucinated, adversary-pre-registered 'phantom' domain is fetched with zero reputation. Article-specific because it scopes rare-domain egress to AI-assistant parent processes, the exact trust surface Unit 42 describes. Rationale: No hard domain IOC exists (Unit 42 redacted the live phantom domains and the build-notifier[.]io URL is explicitly illustrative), so this targets the behavioural core of the article — an AI dev-assistant binary reaching a zero-reputation, never-before-seen external domain — via a 30-day leftanti baseline scoped to named AI-client processes. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adopting a new SaaS/API the AI assistant correctly recommended (real, newly-used domain)
  • AI extension auto-update or telemetry endpoint not yet in baseline
  • First use of a new package registry mirror or docs CDN
  • Newly onboarded host with no 30-day baseline generating many first-seen domains
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".github.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".githubcopilot.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".openai.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".anthropic.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".ollama.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".visualstudio.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the first-seen domain's registration age (WHOIS) and reputation; a domain registered within days that matches a brand's naming pattern is the phantom-squat signal, whereas an established SaaS domain is benign. 2) Contain: if the domain is newly-registered/unreputed, block it at DNS/proxy and warn the developer not to hardcode the URL; capture what data the assistant sent. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same domain, check whether the URL was committed into source/config, and review the AI-assistant session for other hallucinated endpoints.
let AiClients = dynamic(["cursor.exe","code.exe","windsurf.exe","ollama.exe","copilot.exe","continue.exe","claude.exe"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;

| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteIPType == "Public"

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 5) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

let LookbackDays = 7d;

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious PyPI packages give hackers control of Telegram bot servers

BleepingComputer
2026-06-30 6 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A campaign active since last November has been targeting Python developers building Telegram bots with trojanized Pyrogram forks that allow attackers to read arbitrary files on compromised servers. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Operation Navy Ghost: pip install of trojanized Pyrogram fork packages
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Operation Navy Ghost: Python bot spawning /bin/bash -c shell handler · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malicious PyPI packages give hackers control of Telegram bot servers
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Operation Navy Ghost: hidden secret.py backdoor dropped in Pyrogram helpers
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Operation Navy Ghost: bot harvesting /etc/passwd, .env and cloud credentials
Operation Navy Ghost: pip install of trojanized Pyrogram fork packages AIDelivery High
Hunts installation of the eight named malicious Pyrogram forks (vlifegram, pyrogram-styled, pyrogram-navy, etc.) used by Operation Navy Ghost to plant the secret.py Telegram backdoor. Article-specific because it pins the exact PyPI package names the single actor published Nov 2025-Jun 2026, not generic typosquats. Rationale: Uses the eight exact PyPI package names Checkmarx attributes to one Operation Navy Ghost actor; these are not legitimate Pyrogram artifacts so any install command referencing them is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/operation-navy-ghost-pyrogram-telegram-supplychain-attack/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/malicious-pyronut-package-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or malware analyst intentionally pulling a sample of the package into a sandbox
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory sync job that cached the package before takedown re-pulling it during a dependency audit
  • A threat-intel reproduction in a CI pipeline that installs the IOC packages to validate detections
  • A developer searching package names in a string that incidentally lands in a shell history replay
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/opt/sandbox/" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the package name against the IOC list and identify the host/user; check whether the install succeeded and whether the bot process has since started. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the host or the virtualenv, uninstall the package, revoke all Telegram bot tokens issued from that server, and rotate every credential reachable by the bot's service account. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep other build hosts and the private registry for the same package names and for the secret.py artifact (see companion UC), and review outbound Telegram traffic from the affected host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install", "pip3 install", "-m pip install", "pip download", "uv pip install", "poetry add")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vlifegram", "vlife-gram", "kelragram", "pyrogram-navy", "pyrogram-styled", "pyrogram-zeeb", "pyrogram-kelra", "sepgram")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "add")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("vlifegram", "vlife-gram", "kelragram", "pyrogram-navy", "pyrogram-styled", "pyrogram-zeeb", "pyrogram-kelra", "sepgram")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Operation Navy Ghost: hidden secret.py backdoor dropped in Pyrogram helpers AIInstallation High
Hunts the file artifact unique to this campaign: pyrogram/helpers/secret.py, which exists in no legitimate Pyrogram release. Catches the backdoor even when delivered via cache, vendored copy, or private registry rather than a direct pip install. Rationale: secret.py inside pyrogram/helpers is a campaign-unique artifact confirmed by Checkmarx as absent from every legitimate Pyrogram release, making the file path itself a near-deterministic IOC independent of the delivery vector. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/operation-navy-ghost-pyrogram-telegram-supplychain-attack/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/malicious-pyronut-package-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1554 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately named an unrelated local module secret.py and placed it under a directory tree that happens to contain both 'pyrogram' and 'helpers' path components
  • Analyst extraction of the sample to a forensic workstation under a path containing pyrogram/helpers
  • A backup/restore job rewriting an already-infected venv (true positive, but may look like benign file activity)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has "site-packages" or FolderPath has "dist-packages" or FolderPath has "/lib/python"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the secret.py and the sibling __init__.py / methods/utilities/start.py to confirm the exec(compile()) / subprocess /bin/bash -c handlers and the hardcoded OWNERS Telegram IDs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill any running bot process loading the package, delete the venv, and revoke the bot token. Step 3 (hunt): Search all hosts and registries for the same file path, then pivot to outbound Telegram document uploads (reply_document) and python-spawned /bin/bash -c activity from the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "secret.py"
| where FolderPath has "pyrogram" and FolderPath has "helpers"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "secret.py"
| where TargetFilePath has "pyrogram" and TargetFilePath has "helpers"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Operation Navy Ghost: Python bot spawning /bin/bash -c shell handler AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the runtime behaviour of the /asi (/wann2) shell command handler, where the infected Pyrogram bot uses subprocess.run() to spawn /bin/bash -c on attacker-supplied strings. Pivots on a python parent spawning a shell with -c on a production bot host. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated execution chain (python bot -> subprocess.run -> /bin/bash -c), the concrete behaviour of the /asi (/wann2) handler; broad on its own so shipped as hunting tier with FP guidance below. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/operation-navy-ghost-pyrogram-telegram-supplychain-attack/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python apps shelling out (e.g. ansible, docker SDK wrappers, CI runners, supervisord-managed services calling shell helpers)
  • Data-pipeline jobs invoking bash -c for file munging
  • DevOps automation using subprocess to run shell one-liners during deploys
  • Jupyter/IPython '!command' shell escapes on a dev box
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible", "supervisord", "/usr/bin/docker", "gitlab-runner", "jenkins") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/lib/", "dpkg", "apt-get"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child shell command line and the parent python process path; benign hits are usually deterministic deploy/automation commands, malicious ones are ad-hoc reads of secrets or recon (id, uname, env). Step 2 (contain): If the parent python is a Pyrogram/Telegram bot or the command reads credentials, isolate the host and revoke the bot token. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with the secret.py file UC and with the bot reading /etc/passwd/.env (credential UC), and review outbound Telegram document uploads in the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python"
| where FileName in~ ("bash", "sh", "dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "python"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("bash", "sh", "dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Operation Navy Ghost: bot harvesting /etc/passwd, .env and cloud credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-access actions the backdoor performs over its shell/Python handlers: reading /etc/passwd, environment variables (os.environ / printenv), .env files, and cloud credential files from a python- or shell-initiated process. Mirrors the article's '/asi cat /etc/passwd' and os.environ examples. Rationale: Built directly from the article's quoted examples (/asi cat /etc/passwd and /asu print(os.environ)); requiring a python/shell parent plus a sensitive-credential read target keeps this aligned to the backdoor's exfil staging rather than generic file access. Cross-checked against: • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/operation-navy-ghost-pyrogram-telegram-supplychain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Chef/Puppet) templating /etc/passwd or reading .env during deploys
  • Backup or compliance-scanning agents enumerating /etc/passwd and SSH keys
  • Application startup scripts legitimately sourcing a .env file
  • A developer debugging environment variables with printenv on a dev host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible", "puppet", "chef-client", "salt-minion", "/usr/sbin/cron") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Examine the full command line and parent process; a Pyrogram/Telegram bot or an unexpected ad-hoc read of /etc/passwd + .env + cloud creds in quick succession is high-signal, scheduled config jobs are not. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, revoke the Telegram bot token, and rotate every credential the read targeted (DB, cloud API keys, SSH keys, .env secrets). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the secret.py file UC and the python->bash -c UC on the same host, and review outbound Telegram document uploads (reply_document) for the exfiltrated content.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "bash", "sh", "dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", ".aws/credentials", "/proc/self/environ", "printenv", "os.environ", "id_rsa", ".docker/config.json", "/.env")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python", "bash", "sh", "dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", ".aws/credentials", "/proc/self/environ", "printenv", "os.environ", "id_rsa", ".docker/config.json", "/.env")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation or filesystem presence of the trojanized postmark-mcp MCP server (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that the Microsoft article cites as the first real-world malicious MCP server. Catches the supply-chain entry point before the agent ever runs the poisoned tool. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package name postmark-mcp confirmed by Koi Security/Snyk/Postmark; any install of this impersonating package is high-fidelity since Postmark never published it and v1.0.16+ is confirmed backdoored. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://postmarkapp.com/blog/information-regarding-malicious-postmark-mcp-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately testing/evaluating postmark-mcp before the malicious disclosure
  • Internal mirror/proxy npm cache replaying the package name in audit tooling
  • Security researcher reproducing the Koi finding in a sandbox
  • SBOM/dependency-scanning tool string-matching the package name in its own logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe') and not (FolderPath has 'sandbox' or DeviceName has 'sec-research')
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version via package-lock.json / node_modules/postmark-mcp/package.json — v1.0.16 and later are backdoored. Identify the host, user, and whether the MCP server actually ran. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, block npm publisher 'phanpak', and isolate any host/agent that sent live email through it; rotate Postmark API tokens and any credentials ever emailed via the agent. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound mail logs for BCC to giftshop.club (UC2) and sweep all hosts for the node_modules\postmark-mcp path and the domain across DNS/proxy.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source='ProcessCreate', Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @'node_modules\postmark-mcp' or FolderPath contains 'node_modules/postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source='FileWrite', Detail=FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath )
| where AccountName !endswith '$'
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| where SubjectUserName !endswith '$'
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious postmark-mcp npm Package Installation
id: 9f2a4b7c-1d3e-4f5a-8b6c-2e1d0a9f8c7b
status: experimental
description: Detects installation of the trojanized postmark-mcp npm package (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that BCCs all agent-sent email to phan@giftshop.club.
references:
  - https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-warns-poisoned-mcp-tool.html

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*postmark-mcp*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/postmark-mcp/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual exfiltration channel of the postmark-mcp backdoor: every email the agent sends is silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop.club. Surfaces any outbound mail with a recipient/BCC in the giftshop.club domain. Rationale: giftshop.club / phan@giftshop.club is the confirmed BCC exfil sink for postmark-mcp v1.0.16, corroborated by Koi, Snyk, Qualys and Postmark's advisory; any mail to that domain is a direct true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2025/09/30/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-exploited-in-attack/
ATT&CKT1041 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business contact who genuinely uses a giftshop.club address (verify against directory)
  • Marketing/transactional bulk mail accidentally addressed to the domain
  • Threat-intel detonation/sandbox that replays the IOC in a test tenant
  • Phishing-simulation platform seeding the known-bad domain
Suppression filter
| where not (EmailDirection == 'Inbound')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull every message in the hit set, identify the sending mailbox/agent identity and whether messages contain sensitive content (invoices, credentials). Confirm giftshop.club is not a known legitimate partner. 2) Contain: create a transport rule blocking mail to giftshop.club, suspend the implicated agent/service identity, and remove postmark-mcp from the sending host; rotate Postmark tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes/agents that ever sent via postmark-mcp, scope total exfil volume, and check for other phanpak-published packages in the environment.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress has 'giftshop.club' or SenderFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club' or SenderMailFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload has 'Exchange'
| where Recipients has 'giftshop.club' or P2RecipientList has 'giftshop.club'
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, P2RecipientList, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club AICommand & Control Medium
Cross-telemetry sweep for any host resolving or connecting to giftshop.club, the attacker domain behind the postmark-mcp backdoor. Catch-all in case the domain is reused for web callbacks or appears in proxy/DNS where mail telemetry is blind. Rationale: giftshop.club is the confirmed attacker domain (multi-source); a pure-IOC domain sweep across DNS/proxy/network is a cheap catch-all that complements the email-BCC detection where mail telemetry is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/ • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed connectors that beacon IOC domains for reputation lookups
  • Sandbox/detonation infrastructure resolving the known-bad domain
  • Security awareness or phishing-sim platform referencing the domain
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ telemetry logging blocked lookups (already mitigated)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('msmpeng.exe','mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe','filebeat.exe')
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — confirm it is not a security tool doing reputation lookups. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block giftshop.club at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a non-security process initiated the lookup, and check that host for postmark-mcp. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound mail-BCC hits (UC2) and package-install hits (UC1) on the same host, and add giftshop.club to the org blocklist/TI watchlist.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source='DNS' ),
( DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, SrcHostname=Computer, Indicator=Name, Source='DnsEvents' ),
( CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL has 'giftshop.club' or DestinationHostName has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Source='Proxy' )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

RustDuck Botnet Rebuilds in Rust to Hijack Routers and Servers for DDoS

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new two-stage malware family called RustDuck is hijacking home routers, IP cameras, Android boxes, and poorly secured servers, then stitching them into a network built to knock websites and online services offline. Researchers at QiAnXin's&nbsp;XLab&nbsp;have tracked it since February 2026, and say the real story is not how big it is today, but how fast it is changing. The end goal is a

CVEsCVE-2017-17215 CVE-2025-29635 CVE-2024-1781 CVE-2018-8007
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1528
IPs176.65.139.204

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Egress to RustDuck spreader/delivery host 176.65.139.204 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2017-17215 Huawei HG532 TR-064 command injection (RustDuck spread vector) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RustDuck DuckDNS dynamic-DNS C2 resolution/beaconing · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Egress to RustDuck spreader/delivery host 176.65.139.204 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts internal hosts (routers, servers, IoT gateways, or any monitored endpoint) making inbound or outbound connections to 176.65.139.204, XLab's busiest RustDuck malware-distribution address. A device reaching this IP is almost certainly pulling the second-stage Rust core loader. Rationale: Uses the single concrete network IOC from the article — spreader IP 176.65.139.204 — which XLab flagged as the busiest of 20+ distribution addresses; a hard IP match is inherently low-FP. Corroborated by cyberpress.org and techjuice.pk write-ups of the same XLab report. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/rustduck-botnet-expands-attacks/ • https://www.techjuice.pk/rustduck-botnet-rust-routers-servers-ddos-hijack-xlab/
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing the IP
  • Internal threat-intel scanner or ASM tool actively probing known-bad infrastructure
  • Shared bulletproof-hosting block — an unrelated benign service briefly co-located on the same address after takedown
  • Firewall/IDS logging a blocked (not established) connection, which is a true positive of attempted contact but not compromise
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "ConnectionFailed"   // keep only established sessions; blocked probes are informational
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm connection direction and whether it was allowed or blocked at the perimeter; identify the internal asset and whether it is an internet-facing router/IoT/server matching RustDuck's target profile. 2) Contain: block 176.65.139.204 (and the parent /24) egress+ingress at the firewall, and isolate the internal host if the connection was established. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to DNS for *.duckdns.org (UC3) and check for any inbound exploit attempts on TR-064/37215 (UC2); sweep the fleet for any other host that touched the same /24 bulletproof block.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.139.204"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.139.204" or SourceIP == "176.65.139.204"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2017-17215 Huawei HG532 TR-064 command injection (RustDuck spread vector) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST exploitation of CVE-2017-17215 against Huawei HG532 routers — the Mirai-lineage TR-064 firmware-upgrade bug RustDuck sprays to seed new bots. Matches the /ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1 endpoint on port 37215 carrying shell metacharacters in the NewStatusURL/NewDownloadURL SOAP elements. Rationale: Anchors on the unambiguous CVE-2017-17215 exploit signature — POST to /ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1 on port 37215 with NewStatusURL/NewDownloadURL — which the article names as a RustDuck spread vector and which Check Point/SonicWall/exploit-db independently document as the Mirai/Satori payload path. The endpoint string is never legitimate on a non-Huawei network. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty because inbound router exploitation lives in network/WAF telemetry, not EDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2017/good-zero-day-skiddie/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/blog/new-wave-of-attacks-attempting-to-exploit-huawei-home-routers • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/43414
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) firing the CVE-2017-17215 plugin against internal Huawei gear
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement replaying the public PoC
  • Security research honeypot intentionally soliciting the exploit
  • IDS decoding an unrelated benign SOAP TR-064 firmware-upgrade request to a real HG532 without shell metacharacters (rare — pair with the $()/backtick check to eliminate)
Suppression filter
| where Message has_any ("$(", "`", "busybox", "wget", "tftp", "chmod", "/bin/")   // keep only requests carrying an actual injected shell command
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP (external scanner vs. attacker), confirm the request body contains shell metacharacters ($(), backticks, wget/tftp/busybox) in NewStatusURL/NewDownloadURL, and check whether any Huawei HG532/TR-064 device is actually exposed on 37215. 2) Contain: block the source IP, and firewall port 37215 off the public internet for all router assets. 3) Hunt: if a real device was hit, pivot that device's egress to 176.65.139.204 (UC1) and *.duckdns.org (UC3); replace or re-flash EoL routers per CISA guidance since no RustDuck-proof patch exists.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has "/ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1"
    or DestinationPort == 37215
    or Message has_any ("NewStatusURL", "NewDownloadURL", "DeviceUpgrade_1")
| where RequestURL has "/ctrlt/DeviceUpgrade_1"
    or Message has_any ("NewStatusURL", "NewDownloadURL")
    or (DestinationPort == 37215 and RequestMethod =~ "POST")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RustDuck DuckDNS dynamic-DNS C2 resolution/beaconing AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DNS resolutions and connections to *.duckdns.org, the free dynamic-DNS service RustDuck uses for its rotating C2 endpoints (the 'Duck' in the name). Surfaces routers/servers repeatedly resolving duckdns subdomains — especially from non-browser processes — as candidate bot check-ins. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 provider (duckdns.org) as the pivot; scoped to non-browser initiators and aggregated by count to separate periodic bot beaconing from one-off legitimate hobbyist lookups. Kept at hunting tier because duckdns is dual-use. Corroborated by the XLab-based cyberpress.org write-up naming duckdns as the RustDuck control channel. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/rustduck-botnet-expands-attacks/ • https://www.techjuice.pk/rustduck-botnet-rust-routers-servers-ddos-hijack-xlab/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Home-lab / Home Assistant / Pi-hole users pointing remote access at a duckdns hostname
  • Self-hosted game servers, cameras, or VPN endpoints legitimately using DuckDNS
  • Developers testing the open-source duckdns updater client
  • A single benign duckdns lookup with no repeating cadence (filtered out by the count/aggregation)
Suppression filter
| where ConnCount >= 6   // >=6 resolutions in window approximates RustDuck's ~10-min beacon cadence and drops one-off benign lookups
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the resolving host and initiating process — an IoT gateway, Linux server, or a non-browser binary resolving duckdns on a fixed ~10-minute cadence (RustDuck rotates keys every 10 min) is high-suspicion; a workstation browser is likely benign. 2) Contain: sinkhole or block the specific duckdns subdomain(s), and isolate any host showing periodic beaconing. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host against egress to 176.65.139.204 (UC1) and inbound TR-064 exploitation (UC2); capture PCAP to confirm the ChaCha20-Poly1305/AES-GCM TLS-mimicking traffic RustDuck uses.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "duckdns.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,15) by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ConnCount desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith "duckdns.org"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), Subdomains=dcount(Name) by Computer, ClientIP, Name
| order by Queries desc

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

            - '\Cookies'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

Langflow Python endpoint spawning shell to fetch payload via curl/wget (CVE-2026-33017 RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-33017 exploitation chain where an unauthenticated Langflow API endpoint evaluates attacker Python that forks a shell running curl/wget to pull the lambsys dropper. Article-specific because it pins the Langflow/uvicorn/python parent spawning sh -c with a remote-fetch utility. Rationale: Chains the article's explicit description: an unauthenticated Langflow endpoint evaluates Python that 'launches a remotely hosted shell script' fetched with curl or wget. Parent(python/uvicorn)+child(sh)+curl/wget is high-fidelity for this RCE-to-dropper step.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow/Python apps legitimately invoking curl/wget in a subprocess for model or dataset downloads
  • CI/CD deployment scripts run under a gunicorn-managed venv that fetch dependencies
  • Custom Langflow flows that shell out to curl for HTTP integration testing
  • Container entrypoint scripts pulling assets on first boot
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("pip install","requirements.txt","apt-get","model_download")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child cmdline and the fetched URL/IP; confirm the parent Langflow process is internet-exposed and whether the API request that triggered it was unauthenticated. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python/langflow worker and any lambsys child, block egress to the fetched host at the firewall. 3) Hunt: search the same host for lambsys execution, cron edits under /var/spool/cron, and beacons to 83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241; verify Langflow is patched for CVE-2026-33017.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","langflow","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Facility in ("authpriv","user","daemon")
| where ProcessName in~ ("python","python3","langflow","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("sh -c","bash -c")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

lambsys ELF dropper/miner execution and detached launch AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution of the Go ELF binary 'lambsys' (the campaign's dropper/miner loader) by filename, path, or reference in a shell command line, including its detached launch (nohup/setsid/&). Article-specific because 'lambsys' is the named custom binary. Rationale: 'lambsys' is the article's explicitly named custom Go ELF binary that checks if it is already running, launches detached, and loads XMRig. Filename + provided SHA256/MD5 hashes make this an alerting-grade, campaign-specific detection.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1543 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely unlikely benign hit — 'lambsys' is not a standard package name
  • A security tool or sandbox re-running the sample for analysis
  • Backup/AV quarantine paths that retain the binary name in a scan log
  • An internal IR playbook file or note containing the string 'lambsys'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary hash against the three campaign SHA256s and note the executing user/path and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the lambsys process tree, capture the binary for forensics before it self-wipes the extracted XMRig TAR. 3) Hunt: enumerate SSH-reachable hosts from ~/.ssh/known_hosts and authorized_keys for lateral spread, and check for the miner TAR fetch and beacon to 83.142.209.214.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "lambsys" or ProcessCommandLine has "lambsys" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "lambsys"
| where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc","33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df","ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2") or ProcessCommandLine has "lambsys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "lambsys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
