Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts AI-coding-agent-spawned shells running commands obfuscated to defeat plain-text blocklists: empty-quote/backslash-split binary names (r''m), base64 piped into sh/bash, or benign tools (find/dd) given destructive flags. This is the exact GuardFall evasion shape where bash rewrites the string after the agent's filter inspected it. Rationale: Uses the article's literal GuardFall evasion primitives (empty-quote split like r''m, base64-pipe-to-shell, destructive find/dd flags) anchored to the named open-source agent binaries as parents — the combination of agent-parent + shell-child + obfuscated cmdline is far higher-fidelity than any single clause. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1027.010 T1140 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running a build script that base64-decodes an embedded asset and pipes it to a shell installer
  • CI/dev tooling using find -delete to clean build artifacts
  • dd used for legitimate disk imaging by a sysadmin on a dev box
  • Shell aliases or generated scripts that happen to contain quote-adjacent tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","make ","cmake","docker build") and ProcessCommandLine has "-delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64; confirm the parent is an AI coding agent and whether the session was non-interactive/auto-exec. Identify the repo/working dir the agent was pointed at. 2) Contain: kill the agent + shell processes, revoke and rotate any credentials reachable from $HOME (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and quarantine the host from prod networks. 3) Hunt: review the triggering repo/PR (especially fork PRs and in-repo config like .aider.conf.yml) for the injected instruction; sweep other dev hosts for the same agent-parent + obfuscated-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI Coding Agent Shell with Obfuscated Command (GuardFall)
id: 6f3c1d2a-9b4e-4f1a-8c77-2a1e5b9d0c44
description: Detects an AI coding agent spawning a shell whose command line uses GuardFall-style obfuscation (empty-quote split binaries, base64 piped to shell, destructive find/dd flags) to bypass plain-text command blocklists.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/guardfall-exposes-open-source-ai-coding.html
  - https://adversa.ai/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1027.010
  - attack.t1140
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/aider'
      - '/goose'
      - '/cline'
      - '/plandex'
      - '/opencode'
      - '/open-interpreter'
      - '/openhands'
      - '/swe-agent'
      - '/node'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
  selection_shell:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
  selection_obfusc:
    CommandLine|re: "(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\\s+-d.*\\|\\s*(ba)?sh|\\bdd\\s+.+of=/dev/|find\\s+.+-delete|find\\s+.+-exec\\s+rm"
  condition: selection_parent and selection_shell and selection_obfusc
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR zsh)) (@process.command_line:(*"base64 -d"* OR *"-exec rm"* OR *-delete* OR *of=/dev/*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(aider|goose|cline|plandex|opencode|open-interpreter|openhands|swe-agent|node|python3?)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|dash|zsh)$/i
| regex("(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","roo-code","node","python","python3") Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","roo-code","node","python","python3") Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","dash","zsh") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the GuardFall precondition: a named open-source coding agent invoked with an auto-execute / skip-permissions flag (--auto-exec, --auto-run, --auto-test, --yes-always, dangerously-skip-permissions) that then spawns a shell or interpreter non-interactively. This is the unattended configuration that lets an injected command actually run. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit auto-execute flag names (--auto-exec/--auto-run/--auto-test/dangerously-skip-permissions) AND the named agent binaries spawning a shell — the unattended-execution precondition the article says must be true for the attack to land, making it a high-fidelity governance/posture alert. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/01/claude_code_rule_cap_raises/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal CI pipeline that intentionally runs an agent unattended on trusted internal repos
  • Developer using --yes-always on their own local repo for a known refactor
  • Automated test harness invoking the agent with --auto-test against a sandboxed branch
  • Demo/eval scripts running an agent non-interactively in a throwaway container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--auto-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the agent run was sanctioned (internal trusted repo vs fork/external) and which repo/working dir it targeted; capture the child shell command lines. 2) Contain: if the repo source is untrusted or unknown, terminate the agent session and disable the auto-execute flag in the relevant wrapper/CI job; isolate the host pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners running these agents with auto-exec flags, and correlate forward to credential-file reads or outbound connections from the spawned shells.

AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GuardFall credential-theft payload: a shell or copy/transfer tool spawned by an AI coding agent that reads SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other home-folder secrets. Targets the article's stated impact — stealing 'SSH keys and cloud credentials to anything sitting in your home folder'. Rationale: Combines the article's named agent binaries as parent with the exact credential paths it calls out (SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds in $HOME) referenced by a read/copy/transfer child process — agent-spawned access to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws is well outside normal agent working-dir behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately tasked with configuring git over SSH or deploying via scp reading ~/.ssh/config
  • Developer-driven 'aws configure' or terraform run that the agent shells out to and which touches ~/.aws/credentials
  • Backup or dotfile-sync tooling invoked through the agent's shell
  • Agent reading ~/.docker/config.json to run an authorized image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","git@","ssh -T","terraform") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the credential access matched the task the user gave the agent; capture the destination of any subsequent cp/scp/curl. 2) Contain: immediately rotate the specific keys/credentials touched (SSH keypairs, AWS access keys, kube tokens) and revoke sessions; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the same shell for outbound exfil shortly after the read, and review the source repo/PR that the agent was operating on.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout AIDelivery Low
Hunts the GuardFall initial-access vector where a malicious agent config file shipped inside a repository (the article calls out .aider.conf.yml) is written to disk by a VCS/clone or the agent itself, which can trigger the attack on the first accepted edit. Treats in-repo agent config as untrusted code. Rationale: Uses the exact config filename the article names as untrusted-code (.aider.conf.yml) written by a clone/checkout or the agent — a focused hunting pivot for the supply-chain delivery step, kept low-confidence/hunting because legitimate repos also ship this file. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/blog/the-approval-prompt-is-lying-to-you-symlink-rce-in-five-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-cursor-antigravity-copilot-grok-build/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately commits .aider.conf.yml to share project agent settings
  • Developer cloning their own trusted repo that contains the config
  • Templating/scaffolding tools generating an aider config
  • CI checkout of an internal repo that ships the file by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/internal-repos/","/trusted/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the contents of the written .aider.conf.yml for embedded auto-run/auto-commit settings, shell hooks, or instructions, and identify the source repo/PR (especially fork PRs). 2) Contain: if the repo is untrusted/external, prevent the agent from running against it, move $HOME to a throwaway folder per the article's guidance, and disable auto-execute. 3) Hunt: correlate forward to agent-spawned shells (UC1/UC2) and credential reads (UC3) on the same host within the session window.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ (".aider.conf.yml",".aider.conf.yaml","aider.conf.yml")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

What the Numbers Say About FIFA 2026 Cyber Risk

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The FIFA World Cup 2026 opened on June 11. By that date, according to Check Point Research, the fraud infrastructure targeting it had already been built, staged, and partially deployed. Threat actor activity was pre-planned, months out, across three sectors and at least ten languages. Check Point Exposure Management published the FIFA World Cup 2026 Cyber Threat Report this month, covering

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains · [LLM] Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the specific FIFA 2026 brand-impersonation domains staged by the Check Point / Group-IB-tracked fraud infrastructure (hospitality, store, and gambling lures). Article-specific because it pins the named registered domains rather than a generic 'newly-registered domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the seven concrete lookalike domains from the article's IOC bundle (www-fifa.me/.co, 26-fifa.com, op.shop-26fifa.com, fifaofficialstore.shop, fifa2026guess.com, fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn); these are dedicated fraud-only domains so any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the FBI IC3 PSA and Check Point's research blog which independently confirm the campaign and several of the same domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/ • https://www.gblock.app/articles/fifa-2026-phishing-wave-fake-domains-email-scams
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform manually browsing the domain during triage
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox / SOAR enrichment visiting the domain from a known scanning host
  • Secure web gateway pre-fetch or link-rewrite service resolving the URL on the user's behalf
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor crawling the domain from corporate ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-sandbox","svc-urlscan") and DeviceName !in~ ("SOC-SANDBOX01","PROXY-SCAN01")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the host/user and the initiating process from DeviceNetworkEvents — confirm it was a browser/mail client (real user) vs a sandbox/proxy host, and whether a file download or credential-entry POST followed within 5 min. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS and the secure web gateway tenant-wide; if the user submitted data, force a password reset + revoke sessions and isolate the host if a payload landed. 3) HUNT: pivot on the resolved IP and registrar pattern (.top, GoDaddy/Hostinger/Namecheap/Porkbun/IONOS) to surface sibling FIFA lookalikes the same host or org touched; review EmailEvents for the delivering message.
let fifaDomains = dynamic(["www-fifa.me","www-fifa.co","26-fifa.com","shop-26fifa.com","op.shop-26fifa.com","fifaofficialstore.shop","fifa2026guess.com","fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (fifaDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (fifaDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose sender domain (envelope or header-from) or embedded URL belongs to the FIFA World Cup 2026 fraud domains — the article notes a subset have MX records configured for reply-path impersonation and password-reset interception. Article-specific via the named domains rather than a generic spoofing rule. Rationale: Anchors on the same seven named fraud domains but on the mail vector (SenderFromDomain / SenderMailFromDomain / embedded URL), targeting the reply-path-impersonation and password-reset-interception use the article calls out for the MX-enabled subset. Domains corroborated by FBI IC3 and Check Point; mail tracing is uniquely a Defender-for-O365 signal, so other platforms are left blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using a FIFA-themed lure domain that overlaps a string
  • Brand-protection vendor sending sample/takedown-notice mail referencing the domains
  • Threat-intel newsletter or this very article being forwarded internally with the domains in the body (URL match on a benign report)
  • Quarantined/blocked messages surfacing in the hunt even though they never reached a user (DeliveryAction = Blocked/Quarantine)
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","JunkFolder") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishsimvendor.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation — prioritize messages Delivered to Inbox; check whether the recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents) or replied. 2) CONTAIN: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and embedded URL, and if any recipient entered credentials or replied to a reply-path lure, force password reset + revoke tokens. 3) HUNT: search for the same sender infrastructure (shared IP/SPF record) hitting other mailboxes and correlate recipients against the UC1 network/DNS hits to find users who both received and visited the domain.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

author: Clankerusecase

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Attackers Exploit SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 to Deploy TaskWeaver and Djinn Stealer

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown threat actor has been observed exploiting a recently disclosed maximum-severity security flaw in SimpleHelp to deliver two previously unreported malware families, TaskWeaver and Djinn Stealer. The intrusion involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-48558 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical authentication bypass vulnerability impacting the OpenID Connect (OIDC) flow that an unauthenticated

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SimpleHelp RMM service spawning node.exe/script interpreter (CVE-2026-48558 post-exploit) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Attackers Exploit SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 to Deploy TaskWeaver and Djinn Steal
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TaskWeaver Node.js loader: node.exe executing jquery.js · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TaskWeaver C2 beacon to typosquatted Microsoft Dev Tunnels (dev-tunnels.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Djinn Stealer credential-store harvesting by node.exe (cloud/SSH/AI-assistant configs) · [LLM] Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
SimpleHelp RMM service spawning node.exe/script interpreter (CVE-2026-48558 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SimpleHelp remote-access service launching node.exe or a script host, the post-auth command-execution step after CVE-2026-48558 forged-OIDC technician takeover. SimpleHelp's endpoint service legitimately runs Java helper code, never Node.js or shells, so this parent-child pair is the exploitation fingerprint. Rationale: Pairs the article's exploited product (SimpleHelp RMM, CVE-2026-48558) with its confirmed endpoint service binaries/paths (SimpleService.exe, Manage Remote Access Service.exe, JWrapper-Remote Access) as parent of node.exe — the documented TaskWeaver delivery runtime. Parent+child both pinned makes it high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/ • https://github.com/anvilogic-forge/armory/blob/main/detections/endpoint/simplehelp_remote_access_tool_execution/simplehelp_remote_access_tool_execution-splunk-edr.yml • https://www.file.net/process/simpleservice.exe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MSP technician running ad-hoc PowerShell/cmd scripts on managed endpoints via SimpleHelp
  • Approved software-deployment scripts pushed through the RMM toolbox
  • IT automation that legitimately bundles a Node.js helper executed by node.exe
  • Patch/inventory routines spawning wscript/cscript from the RMM agent
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("Get-Inventory","\\RMM\\scripts\\") and AccountName in~ ("svc-rmm","msp-automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; confirm whether node.exe is executing a file named jquery.js (UC2) and whether the technician session that drove it maps to a known MSP staff login or a forged/self-registered OIDC technician on the SimpleHelp server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, suspend the SimpleHelp server's OIDC auth (or block the server externally) and revoke/disable the rogue technician account; confirm CVE-2026-48558 patch level. 3) Hunt: sweep all RMM-managed endpoints for node.exe+jquery.js, connections to dev-tunnels.com, and 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("SimpleService.exe","Manage Remote Access Service.exe","Remote Access.exe")) or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\JWrapper-Remote Access\", @"\JWrapper-Remote Support\"))
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\SimpleService.exe", @"\Manage Remote Access Service.exe", @"\Remote Access.exe", @"\JWrapper-Remote Access\", @"\JWrapper-Remote Support\")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\node.exe", @"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SimpleHelp Remote Access Service Spawning Script Interpreter
id: 9f3b1c42-7a6e-4e21-9b2d-1c5e8a0f4d11
status: experimental
description: Detects the SimpleHelp RMM remote-access service spawning node.exe or a script interpreter, as seen in CVE-2026-48558 exploitation deploying TaskWeaver.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
  - https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1219
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\SimpleService.exe'
      - '\Manage Remote Access Service.exe'
      - '\Remote Access.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\SimpleService.exe OR *\\simpleservice.exe OR *\\JWrapper-Remote\ Access\\* OR *\\JWrapper-Remote\ Support\\*)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\node.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(simpleservice|manage remote access service|remote access)\.exe$/i OR ParentImageFileName=/JWrapper-Remote (Access|Support)/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(node|cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta)\.exe$/i

TaskWeaver Node.js loader: node.exe executing jquery.js AIInstallation High
Hunts node.exe executing a script named jquery.js — the exact TaskWeaver loader disguise reported by Blackpoint. jquery.js is a browser library that is never legitimately run by the Node.js interpreter, making node.exe+jquery.js a near-zero-FP signature. Rationale: Uses the article's literal TaskWeaver tradecraft — 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. A browser library name passed to the Node.js runtime is a contradiction in legitimate use, giving a clean single-event alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer deliberately running a Node test harness file they happened to name jquery.js
  • A frontend build/bundler step that shells out node against a vendored jquery.js (rare — usually bundlers read it, not exec it)
  • Security testing/red-team replaying this exact TTP in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\") and ProcessCommandLine has "--test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: collect the node.exe SHA256, full command line, the jquery.js path and its parent process; confirm whether the parent is the SimpleHelp service (UC1) or a temp/AppData drop. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node.exe tree, and quarantine the jquery.js artifact for reversing. 3) Hunt: on the same host and across managed fleet, look for the C2 callout to dev-tunnels.com (UC3), credential-store access by node.exe (UC4), and exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TaskWeaver C2 beacon to typosquatted Microsoft Dev Tunnels (dev-tunnels.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution/connection to a.dev-tunnels.com, TaskWeaver's encrypted C2 channel. The legitimate Microsoft service is devtunnels.ms; the hyphenated .com form is a deliberate typosquat, so any contact with dev-tunnels.com is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 host a.dev-tunnels.com. External research confirms it is a typosquat of Microsoft Dev Tunnels (legit = *.devtunnels.ms), so the hyphenated .com pattern alone is malicious and won't collide with genuine Dev Tunnels traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/attack-exploiting-simplehelp-vulnerability-deploys-novel-loader-infostealer
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected for the exact dev-tunnels.com string; the legitimate service is devtunnels.ms and would not match
  • Internal threat-intel/sandbox detonation hosts deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Security researcher visiting the domain in a browser during analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process (node.exe expected per DeviceNetworkEvents); correlate to a node.exe+jquery.js execution (UC2) in the prior minutes. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block dev-tunnels.com at DNS and egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: across the fleet for any dev-tunnels.com resolution and for subsequent exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5); review which credentials the host could reach (cloud, SCM, AI tools) for forced rotation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Djinn Stealer credential-store harvesting by node.exe (cloud/SSH/AI-assistant configs) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the TaskWeaver node.exe runtime touching multiple distinct developer credential stores in one process — .aws/.azure/gcloud/.oci, .ssh, gh CLI, Docker, npmrc, AI-assistant configs (Claude/Codex/Cline/OpenCode), and crypto wallets. The breadth across cloud+SCM+AI+wallet stores in a single node.exe is the Djinn Stealer collection fingerprint. Rationale: Enumerates the exact credential-store set the article attributes to Djinn Stealer (AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI, gh CLI, Docker, npm, .ssh, AI assistants Claude/Codex/Cline/OpenCode, crypto wallets), and requires >=3 distinct stores touched by a single node.exe to separate stealer fan-out from a developer reading one config. Caveat: file-read telemetry is partial on Defender (reads not always logged); Falcon FileOpenInfo gives the cleanest read visibility, hence hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/djinn-stealer-targets-cloud-ai-credentials • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://devops.com/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-flaw-to-steal-info-from-ai-coding-assistants-clouds/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Node-based dev tool (e.g. an IaC CLI or AI coding agent) legitimately reading .aws + .ssh + .docker during normal work
  • CI/build agents running node that load multiple registry/cloud creds
  • Backup/sync software wrapping node touching dotfile config dirs
  • A developer's terminal AI assistant enumerating its own .config on startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("build","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node.exe maps to TaskWeaver (jquery.js cmdline/UC2) rather than a legit Node CLI; list the exact credential paths touched and timestamps. 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat every touched credential as compromised — immediately rotate cloud keys, SSH keys, gh/PATs, npm tokens, vault tokens, and move crypto wallet funds. 3) Hunt: check the rotated credentials' cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/AzureActivity) for use from attacker IPs, and look for exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.oci\", @"\.ssh\", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\", @"\.kube\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.anthropic\", @"\.config\Claude\", @"\.codex\", @"\.cline\", @"\.config\opencode\", @"\.vault-token", @"\Electrum\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Bitcoin\")
| summarize PathCount = dcount(FolderPath), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathCount >= 3   // breadth across >=3 distinct credential stores = stealer fan-out, not a dev touching one config
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.oci\", @"\.ssh\", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\", @"\.kube\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.anthropic\", @"\.config\Claude\", @"\.codex\", @"\.cline\", @"\.config\opencode\", @"\Electrum\", @"\Exodus\")
| summarize PathCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId
| where PathCount >= 3   // >=3 distinct credential stores touched by one node.exe
| order by FirstSeen desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true), as=store_count)
| store_count >= 3

Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the article's attacker exfil endpoint 96.126.130.126 on TCP 58942 — the destination where Djinn Stealer ships its AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048 encrypted TAR.GZ of harvested credentials. A fixed IP on a high non-standard port is a near-zero-FP exfil indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exfil socket 96.126.130.126:58942 (the AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048 TAR.GZ drop). A hardcoded IP plus uncommon high port is unambiguous; matching either platform's network telemetry yields an immediate, low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1048 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal sandbox/threat-intel detonation host deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC validation or firewall block-rule testing against the IP
  • Shared egress/proxy IP coincidentally NATed to this destination (verify the destination, not the source)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (node.exe expected) and the source host/user; estimate bytes_out to gauge how much was exfiltrated. 2) Contain: block 96.126.130.126 at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and capture the node.exe and any staged TAR.GZ for forensics. 3) Hunt: rotate ALL credentials the host could reach (cloud, SCM, npm/registry, SSH, vault, AI-assistant tokens) and review their downstream audit logs for attacker use, since the article warns stolen creds enable later access into prod/build/cloud tenants.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "96.126.130.126" and RemotePort == 58942
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "96.126.130.126" and DestinationPort == 58942
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2

Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"\TaskCache\" and RegistryKey has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence=RegistryKey, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Activity, EventID, EventData
